title: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PXF): The Microfibrillopathy Masterclass
summary: Pseudoexfoliation Syndrome (PXF) is a systemic, age-related microfibrillopathy characterized by the deposition of white, dandruff-like fibrillar material throughout the anterior segment and visceral organs. It is the most common identifiable cause of open-angle glaucoma worldwide, presenting unique challenges in both medical management and phacoemulsification surgery.

sections.title: Definition & Overview
sections.content: Pseudoexfoliation (PXF) is a generalized ordered proteolysis disorder. It involves the production and progressive accumulation of an abnormal fibrillar extracellular material. While visually most prominent on the anterior lens capsule, it is a systemic condition affecting the heart, lungs, liver, and kidneys. Clinically, it manifests as white flaky material on the pupillary margin and lens, leading to secondary open-angle glaucoma (PXG) and significant zonular instability.

sections.title: The Ocular 'Bull's Eye' Anatomy
content: Central Disk: Translucent zone on the anterior lens capsule.
Intermediate Clear Zone: Created by the mechanical rubbing of the iris during miosis/mydriasis.
Peripheral Granular Zone: Often only visible after maximal pupillary dilation; shows a 'hoarfrost' appearance.
Pupillary Margin: White flakes resembling dandruff ('moth-eaten' appearance).
Iris Sphincter: Atrophy leading to 'moth-eaten' transillumination defects at the ruff.

sections.title: Gonioscopy Findings
content: Sampaolesi Line: Pigment deposition anterior to Schwalbe's line.
Hyperpigmentation: Dense, dark, 'tobacco-dust' pigment in the trabecular meshwork.
Narrow Angles: Occurs in ~15% due to anterior lens displacement (zonular laxity).
Dandruff-like flecks in the angle.

sections.title: Pseudoexfoliative Glaucoma (PXG) Profile
content: More aggressive than POAG with higher mean IOP and larger diurnal fluctuations.
Faster rate of progression and greater optic nerve damage at presentation.
Poorer response to medical therapy compared to POAG.
High risk of unilateral presentation initially, with high conversion rate of the fellow eye.

sections.title: Surgical Red Flags: The 'Phaco Nightmare'
content: Poor Pupillary Dilation (Miosis) due to iris stromal fibrosis.
Zonular Dehiscence and Phacodonesis (Lens wobbling).
Spontaneous Lens Subluxation.
Increased risk of Vitreous Loss and Dropped Nucleus.
Capsular Phimosis and IOL Decentration post-operatively.
Corneal Endothelial Vulnerability.

sections.title: Intraoperative Management Protocol
content: Step 1: Mechanical Pupil Expansion (Iris hooks or Malyugin Ring).
Step 2: Liberal use of Cohesive OVD to stabilize the lens and expand the pupil.
Step 3: Carefully sized Capsulorhexis (Not too small, to prevent phimosis).
Step 4: Gentle Hydrodissection (Avoid over-pressurizing the bag).
Step 5: Capsular Tension Ring (CTR) insertion early if zonular instability is noted.
Step 6: Slow-motion Phacoemulsification with reduced parameters.
Step 7: Consider 3-piece IOL if sulcus fixation is required due to posterior capsule rupture.

rows: Mid-peripheral transillumination, younger myopes, Krukenberg spindle.
No PXF material, lower IOP spikes, normal zonules.
Glass wool vitreous opacities, systemic amyloid signs.

sections.title: Management Strategy
content: Medical: Prostaglandins are 1st line; Aqueous suppressants (Beta-blockers/CAIs) for spikes.
Laser: SLT (Selective Laser Trabeculoplasty) is highly effective due to heavy pigmentation but carries higher risk of post-laser IOP spikes.
Surgical: Trabeculectomy or Tube Shunts have higher failure rates than in POAG; MIGS is an emerging option.

sections.title: Investigation & Workup
content: 1. Dilated Slit Lamp Exam (Gold Standard).
2. Gonioscopy (Vital for grading angle and pigment).
3. Pachymetry (CCT often thinner or normal).
4. Optic Nerve Imaging (OCT RNFL/GCC).
5. Visual Field (24-2 SITA Standard).
6. UBM (if zonular dialysis is suspected).

sections.title: Landmark Study: EMGT
sections.content: The Early Manifest Glaucoma Trial (EMGT) sub-analysis revealed that PXF is a strong independent risk factor for progression. Patients with PXF progressed twice as fast as those with POAG. Each 1 mmHg of IOP reduction reduced the risk of progression by approximately 10%.

sections.title: Complications & Prognosis
content: Late IOL-Capsular bag complex dislocation (can occur 5-15 years post-op).
Corneal decompensation due to endothelial PXF deposition.
Higher incidence of Posterior Capsule Opacification (PCO).
Prognosis: Guarded for PXG; requires frequent monitoring of IOP and Visual Fields (every 3-4 months).
